background.definition: Pleurisy is chest pain secondary to inflammation of the serous membranes which lie between the lungs and the chest wall. There are multiple possible causes. The pain typically caused by pleurisy is called "pleuritic chest pain".

list.listitem: See Differential Diagnosis table for causes of pleuritic chest pain.
Cytokines and other mediators of inflammation are released in the pleural spaces. These inflammatory mediators stimulate local somatic pain receptors.

Inflammation of the ribcage pleura or lateral diaphragm is sensed by intercostal nerves. Central diaphragmatic inflammation is felt in the ipsilateral neck or shoulder. The visceral pleura has no pain receptors.
Patients with pleurisy typically complain of pain on inspiration or coughing that worsens with palpation or position change. C
Use validated decision rules for pulmonary embolism and cardiovascular disease to assess risk for those conditions. B
Consider CXR, ECG, and a D-dimer test for patients at risk of cardiopulmonary disease because of age or risk factors. C

list.listitem: Pleurisy is chest pain, usually sharp, caused by inspiration or cough and usually aggravated by palpation or positional change.

Ask about onset, duration, location, quality, and any radiation of pain, as well as what makes it better or worse. Ask about any cardiovascular symptoms (diaphoresis, palpitations, nausea) or pulmonary symptoms (dyspnea, sputum production), as well as about constitutional symptoms (fever, chills, sweats, myalgias) and about recent trauma, exercise, or injury.

On examination, check radial pulses (if uneven suspect aneurysm), and perform a careful cardiopulmonary exam to evaluate for unstable angina or MI, aneurysm, pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax, and costochondritis.

Chest wall pain: A large prospective study found that in primary care patients with chest pain, a final diagnosis of chest wall syndrome was more likely in those with localized muscle tension, stinging pain, pain reproducible by palpation, and absence of cough.

Acute coronary syndrome (ACS) or acute myocardial infarction (AMI): traditionally described as central, pressure-like or tightening, often accompanied by nausea, vomiting, diaphoresis and dyspnea. Pain that is not pleuritic and no pain with chest wall palpation increase the likelihood of MI or unstable angina, but patients with pleuritic chest pain can still have unstable coronary disease.

Pulmonary embolism (PE): patients usually accompanied by tachypnea and/or dyspnea and has a sudden onset; patients may have history of malignancy or previous thromboembolism. They may also have accompanying leg pain or swelling. Use a validated clinical decision rule like the Wells, PERC, revised PISA, or revised Geneva score to evaluate the patient. The presence of pleuritic chest pain only increases the likelihood of PE slightly in patients with suspected PE.

Respiratory infection: In patients with cough, sputum production, and/or fever order a CXR and consider PPD if risk factors or prolonged history of symptoms. Whether or not pain is pleuritic has little effect on the likelihood of pneumonia.
Aortic dissection: patients typically report sudden onset, radiating to back and describe pain as extremely severe in intensity. Patients may have unequal radial pulses or hypotension.
Pneumothorax: patients typically have sudden onset of dyspnea, and may have a history of previous episodes.
Postcardiac injury syndrome follows surgery or trauma is pleuritic and may be accompanied by fever and abnormal CXR with pericardial or pleural effusions.
Suspect Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome in women with pelvic inflammatory disease or STI and pleutic chest pain, typically right-sided.

Patients at low risk for cardiopulmonary disease (i.e. 25 year old patient with isolated pleuritic chest pain and no other important symptoms) do not require diagnostic testing, especially if there is a good explanation for the pain such as respiratory infection or recent trauma/exercise.
For other patients, ECG, chest radiograph, and if PE is suspected d-dimer should be part of the initial evaluation.

In patients with pleuritic chest pain and normal CXR who are acutely ill, bedside lung ultrasound was helpful in one Italian series of 90 patients. Lung ultrasound is also helpful for pneumothorax diagnosis.

Consider testing for tuberculosis, especially in patients at risk such as recent immigrants from countries where the disease is more common. An ELISA test for pleural tuberculosis is accurate (LR+ 8.2, LR− 0.11).

A systematic review of 12 studies with 1022 patients found that tumor necrosis factor-alpha assay of the pleural effusion fluid is also an accurate test for diagnosis of pleural tuberculous (85% sensitive, 80% specific, LR+ 4.2, LR- 0.19, AUC 0.89).

If the diagnosis remains uncertain, thoracic ultrasound guided pleural biopsy may help establish the diagnosis. A systematic review reported sensitivity of 78% for malignancy and 80% for tuberculosis.

A clinical decision rule has been developed and validated in the primary care setting to determine the likelihood of CAD as a cause of chest pain. Chest pain not reproducible by palpation is an important factor.

A study identified the presence of pleuritic chest pain, tenderness over the anterior hepatic border, worsening pain in the right lateral position and a sed rate > 30 mm/hr as having a 75% positive predictive value for Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome.
In evaluating the patient presenting with pleuritic chest pain, always consider serious causes such as acute coronary syndrome, pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax, and aortic dissection.
Validated clinical decision rules for pulmonary embolism and coronary artery disease in patients presenting with chest pain can help risk stratify patients and guide further evaluation.
Initial diagnostic testing usually includes chest radiograph, ECG, and d-dimer test.

See chapters on pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, thoracic aortic aneurysm, and acute myocardial infarction for further details on evaluation for those diagnoses. See also chapter on general approach to the patient with chest pain.

list.listitem: Treatment for pleurisy of benign cause is NSAIDs and other pain control as needed. B
Otherwise treat the underlying cause as indicated. C
NSAIDS can be given for pain, although clinical trial data are very limited.
Narcotic medications can be used for severe pain.
Treat the underlying cause of pleurisy.

In patients with tuberculous pleurisy and effusion, a Cochrane review of 6 RCTs with 590 participants concluded that corticosteroids improve some intermediate measures (effusion size, pleural thickening) but not clinical outcomes (mortality, symptoms).
Consider performing thoracentisis to remove fluid for diagnosis and comfort care.
Consider pleurodesis for recurrent effusions.
Pleural biopsy, thoracoscopy, bronchoscopy and other procedures may be neccesary for accurate diagnosis of the underlying cause.
Consider referral to a psychologist or psychiatrist for the patient suspected of somatoform disorders.
Pleurisy from benign self limited causes should resolve for most patients in 2 to 3 weeks. C
For patients with typical pleurisy associated with viral infection or other benign source, no follow needed unless symptons are unresolved at 3 weeks or new problems develop. C
For patients with significant pathology and secondary disease, follow as recommended for specific disease process. C
